statedGuarantee: SEAgent claims to prevent 'privilege escalation' in LLM agent systems, defined as any agent invocation action outside the oracle-minimal set required by the user's query. Operationally the framework maintains a per-round directed 'System View' graph of users, agents, tools and RAG databases; each agent, tool and RAG database carries statically assigned attributes (Object, Action, Sensitivity, Privacy, Integrity for tools; Integrity for agents; Integrity/Privacy for databases); a Decision Engine matches SELinux-style policies (Goal / Path / Rule) against that graph on every observed tool invocation and returns allow, deny or ask. Four policies are shipped, covering indirect prompt injection, email-based exfiltration, RAG poisoning, and confused-deputy/untrusted-agent flows. It additionally claims per-user non-interference via context, System-View and SEMemory isolation.
advertisedRhetoric: "a mandatory access control (MAC) framework built upon attribute-based access control (ABAC)"; "SEAgent employs a policy-driven Mandatory Access Control (MAC) mechanism to enforce fine-grained rules over the execution flow graph of the agent system"; "We propose SEAgent, a defense framework that enforces mandatory security policies for LLM agent systems." The OS register is reinforced throughout: policies are "inspired by SELinux (Smalley et al., 2001)", the Action attribute uses "terminology aligned with Linux file permissions", the Privacy/Integrity labels are "inspired by the classic information security models like Bell-LaPadula and Biba", and the threat framing is Linux/Android privilege escalation, confused deputy and collusion.
tierSpan: Assumption 1: Tools are provided by a trusted SDK. [...] If no policies are matched after checking the entire database, the engine defaults to allowing the action.
cheapestDefeat: GUARANTEE: no action reaching a sensitive effector executes unless the Decision Engine has matched the resulting System-View path against the Policy DB and returned allow. MECHANISM THAT MUST FAIL: the Decision Engine's interposition on the agent framework's tool-invocation and inter-agent-message path -- an in-process application component inside the orchestrator, consulted only when a declared tool of the trusted SDK is invoked. CHEAPEST ADVERSARY ACTION: reach the effector through any path that never surfaces as a declared tool-invocation edge in the System View. Three concrete forms, in ascending cost, all far below a kernel exploit: (a) a tool whose implementation performs a second, undeclared effect internally -- one node is added to the graph, and everything the tool's own code does (a file write, an outbound HTTP call, a spawned process and its descendants) is invisible to the engine, because Assumption 1 makes the SDK trusted rather than mediated; (b) exploit the fail-open default -- 'the engine defaults to allowing the action' -- so any flow shape the four shipped policies do not name executes unchecked; (c) exploit the static, LLM-assigned labels: labels are assigned once by o1 plus a human reviewer and 'cannot be updated dynamically at runtime', so a tool mislabeled LOW sensitivity or TRUSTED integrity silently disables every policy predicated on it (the authors' own false-positive discussion shows the label is the switch: 'labeling the Wiki tool as TRUSTED would prevent such cases'). TIER OF THE DEFEATED MECHANISM: an application-level chokepoint in the agent runtime. There is no kernel module, no LSM, no seccomp/netns/namespace bound, no label store or reference monitor below the Python process, and no OS object is labeled -- the 'subjects' being labeled are agents, tools and vector databases, i.e. application objects. Nothing prevents a process running the agent from doing what the policy forbids; only the framework's own call site is guarded. Therefore T3, not T2, and emphatically not the kernel-grade MAC the term denotes.
placementSpan: In particular, the adversary can manipulate the system's inputs and untrusted components [...] without the ability to directly interfere with the runtime execution (e.g., modifying model weights or agent actions).

coverageSpans.E1: WRITE: Modify system state or content (e.g., updating configurations, deleting files).
coverageSpans.E2: EXECUTE: Perform a function that triggers observable behavior (e.g., sending messages or executing transactions).
coverageSpans.E3: EXTERNAL: The tool interacts with external APIs or web services. [...] It blocks flows in which an agent reads sensitive personal data and attempts to exfiltrate it via the email sending tool.
coverageSpans.E5: we consider a scenario in which a user installs a web browser application from a third-party repository.
coverageSpans.E6: PERSONAL: Sensitive personal information (e.g., health records, schedules, passwords), guided by GDPR Article 9
coverageSpans.E7: This policy prohibits untrusted agents from invoking any tool with sensitivity above LOW. The use of wildcards in the path pattern ensures that indirect privilege escalation paths, such as confused deputy scenarios, are also covered.

schneider.surrogate: A monitorable safety property over the framework's own observation of execution: deny any declared tool invocation or inter-agent message whose path through the current System View graph matches a prohibited attribute pattern in the Policy DB. This is a per-step, prefix-decidable predicate on an observed trace and is exactly what the Decision Engine enforces -- 'A policy is triggered only when both the path pattern is matched in the System View and the rule expression evaluates to true.'
schneider.objective: Two non-monitorable objectives are advertised over that surrogate. (1) Least privilege: 'we define a privilege escalation attack as any agent actions beyond those minimally required to fulfill the user's intent' -- and the paper concedes the referent is uncomputable in deployment: 'T_q is oracle-defined and often not known in advance, making defense against such attacks challenging.' A monitor cannot decide membership in an oracle set, so five coarse attribute policies stand in for it. (2) Non-interference, an explicit information-flow hyperproperty: 'SEAgent enforces user-level non-interference via user-level isolation' and 'This architecture guarantees non-interference among users.' Non-interference is not a safety property and is not enforceable by an execution monitor; what is actually enforced is per-user partitioning of context, System View and SEMemory, argued informally, with the direct-prompt-injection vector removed from the experiments on the strength of that argument ('we omit further experiments for this vector').

notes:
HEADLINE DEMOTION ROW. The paper's title and abstract advertise a 'Mandatory Access Control Framework'. MAC is a term with precise kernel meaning: a system-wide label store, a reference monitor below the subject, and enforcement the subject cannot decline. SEAgent has none of the three. Its 'subjects' are agents, tools and RAG databases -- application objects, not processes; its label store is a static table produced by OpenAI o1 plus human review; its reference monitor is a Python Decision Engine sitting on the framework's own tool-dispatch path, guarded by Assumption 1 ('Tools are provided by a trusted SDK'), which converts the SDK from a mediated boundary into a trusted one. Nothing below the process is touched. The correct label for the mechanism is an application-level, graph-pattern policy chokepoint over declared tool calls -- a genuinely useful T3 construct, misnamed with T2 vocabulary and dressed in SELinux, Bell-LaPadula, Biba and Linux-file-permission borrowings.

TIER, EXPLICITLY. Guarantee: denied information flows do not execute. Mechanism: in-process interposition at the tool-call site. Cheapest defeat: any effect achieved without producing a declared tool-invocation edge -- most cheaply, effects performed inside a tool's own implementation, whose internals are trusted rather than observed. Defeating that costs no exploit, no forged label and no kernel bug. T3, weakest-link.

FAIL-OPEN. The Decision Engine's default is Allow ('If no policies are matched after checking the entire database, the engine defaults to allowing the action'), and only four policies are shipped ('we do not take credits for their exhaustiveness'). Enforcement is therefore an enumerated denylist over flow shapes, not a mandatory allowlist -- another respect in which the MAC label is inapt.

COVERT-CHANNEL RULE APPLIED. Every effector cell below is capped at partial or worse because the framework's stated contract excludes the channel through which the effector is reachable: whatever a trusted-SDK tool does internally, and whatever any process descended from it does.

EFFECTOR NOTES.
E1 file write = partial. The Action taxonomy names file modification explicitly ('WRITE: Modify system state or content (e.g., updating configurations, deleting files)'), and a declared write tool crossing an UNFILTERED-source path is blocked by the indirect-prompt-injection policy. But there is no filesystem interposition: no path scoping, no rename/unlink distinction, no mediation of writes performed inside a tool implementation, and the default is allow for any flow shape not matching a shipped policy. Provably reaches some instances, provably not others.
E2 subprocess spawn = not-covered. Subprocess, process, fork, exec and descendant appear nowhere in the paper; no benchmark tool spawns a process; no attribute distinguishes a process from an API call. The nearest span, 'EXECUTE: Perform a function that triggers observable behavior (e.g., sending messages or executing transactions)', is an abstract action label over tool semantics, not process creation. Even the most generous reading -- that a hypothetical shell tool would appear as one graph node -- would still cap at partial under the depth rule, since descendants are wholly unmediated; but as the paper does not address the effector at all, the correct code is not-covered.
E3 network egress = partial. Some declared egress is genuinely mediated: EXTERNAL is a first-class Object value, and the Email Data Stealing Protection Policy blocks a PERSONAL-read followed by a send. But egress performed inside a tool implementation, by a subprocess, or by any path the four policies do not name is unmediated and defaults to allow. Descendant egress is not addressed anywhere.
E4 VCS push = not-covered. No VCS, git, repository-push or commit surface appears; the four benchmarks (InjecAgent, AgentDojo, API-Bank, AWS) contain no such tool.
E5 package install = not-covered. The paper discusses third-party AGENT installation from an Agent Hub, but the installation event is not mediated -- SEAgent's response is to label the resulting agent UNFILTERED after the fact. Package managers, install hooks and hook-time network activity are never mentioned. An Uninstall_App tool appears in one worked example, but that is a mediated tool call, not mediation of an install pipeline.
E6 credential use = partial, and capped by rule. Credentials appear only as an example inside the Privacy attribute ('e.g., health records, schedules, passwords'). There is no published credential list: environment variables, config files, keychains and cloud metadata endpoints are never enumerated, and no policy names a credential class. Per the E6 rule, an undefined list caps at partial; the flow-shaped email-exfiltration policy is what makes it partial rather than not-covered.
E7 sub-agent spawn = partial. Inter-agent messages are first-class in the model (tau_aa) and become System-View edges, and the confused-deputy policy uses wildcards to catch indirect delegation, which is real mediation of agent-to-agent invocation -- the paper's strongest result (0% ASR on the AIOS-AutoGen confused-deputy PoC). But the CREATION of an agent is not mediated: a third-party agent is installed outside the framework and only afterwards assigned an Integrity label, labels are static and 'cannot be updated dynamically at runtime', and an agent whose provenance the labeler never sees has no defined label. Delegation is mediated; spawning is not.

EVIDENCE GRADE L2. Behavioral confirmation: 0% ASR reported across the extended InjecAgent and AgentDojo suites, working PoC confused-deputy attacks against AIOS-AutoGen, standard AutoGen and AIOS-MetaGPT, utility measured on API-Bank and the AWS benchmark, and an artifact referenced under Open Science. Not L3: no reproducible bypass of SEAgent itself is demonstrated in the paper. The demonstrated bypasses are of OTHER systems (SecAlign, IsolateGPT Hub- and anonymous-Spoke-level, CaMeL argument hijacking) -- those are L3 findings about the baselines, not about SEAgent.

PLACEMENT. Primary A2: the evaluation actually tests adversary content in tool returns and RAG retrievals (indirect prompt injection, RAG poisoning) -- 'the adversary can inject malicious content into the user query [...] or poison the external environment to manipulate tool returns [...] and RAG retrieval results'. Secondary A3: a third-party agent carrying an adversarial system prompt is addressed and PoC-attacked, but the defense against it is a static provenance label rather than a tested containment of a compromised policy -- 'By crafting malicious system prompts or configurations for these agents, the adversary can indirectly control their generated actions'. Secondary A1: direct prompt injection by a malicious user is claimed to be handled by user-level isolation but is deliberately NOT tested ('we omit further experiments for this vector'). A4 and A5 are excluded by the threat model, which is the load-bearing exclusion for the tier: an adversary inside the harness process, or below it, is assumed away, and that is precisely the adversary a real MAC mechanism exists to bound.

WHERE I WAS UNCERTAIN. (1) E2: an argument exists that a declared shell tool would be visible to the graph, which would make E2 partial rather than not-covered; I coded not-covered because the paper never contemplates process execution and the coding rule states that a system which simply does not address an effector scores not-covered. An adjudicator who reads the tool abstraction as generic enough to include a shell should raise E2 to partial -- but not above it, since descendants are unmediated either way. (2) advertisedTier: the paper never explicitly claims an OS or kernel mechanism, so 'unclear' is defensible; I coded T2 because 'mandatory access control' is a term of art denoting kernel-enforced labeling, the paper reaches for it in the title, and reinforces it with SELinux, Bell-LaPadula, Biba and Linux-permission analogies -- that is a T2 advertisement whether or not a T2 mechanism was ever intended. (3) E7: whether third-party agent installation counts as sub-agent spawn is a judgment call; I treated delegation as mediated and creation as not, yielding partial.
